analysis.one_liner: Eliminates capital gains taxes, cuts the top corporate rate, and creates a Treasury loan fund for banks with troubled assets.
analysis.headline: A bill to eliminate capital gains taxes, cut the top corporate rate to 28%, and lend to banks with distressed assets got no cosponsors, no committee action, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced days after the 2008 financial crisis bailout bill became law, this bill would have set the capital gains tax rate at zero for individuals and corporations, cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 28%, and created a Treasury fund making low-interest loans to banks holding distressed assets. It also would have raised deposit insurance from $100,000 to $250,000 and let banks treat losses on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock as ordinary losses for tax purposes. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy investors would pay no tax on capital gains; large corporations would see their top rate drop to 28%; and banks — especially those holding soured mortgage assets or Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock — would get cheap government loans and larger tax deductions for their losses.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a 0% capital gains rate for both individuals and corporations, and repeals the scheduled expiration of the 2003 capital gains rate cuts [S2] [S3].
Eliminates the two top corporate tax brackets and lowers the maximum corporate rate from 35% to 28% [S2] [S3].
Establishes a Distressed Assets Loan Fund at the Treasury to make low-interest loans to depository institutions holding distressed assets, on terms the Treasury Secretary would set [S2] [S3].
Raises federal deposit insurance and credit union share insurance from $100,000 to $250,000 per account, protecting savers at insured institutions [S2] [S3].

Allows banks to treat gains and losses on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock as ordinary income or loss, making large losses on that stock deductible against ordinary income rather than limited capital losses [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the uncosted revenue loss from eliminating capital gains taxes and cutting corporate rates, and through exposure to losses if the Treasury's loan fund lent to failing banks and was not repaid.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the capital gains tax and cutting the top corporate rate to 28% would reduce federal revenue substantially, with most of the benefit going to households and firms that own stocks and other capital assets [S2] [S3].

The Distressed Assets Loan Fund would lend at low rates to banks holding distressed assets, with terms set by the Treasury Secretary under regulations the Secretary would write, leaving taxpayers exposed if those loans went unpaid [S3].
Raising deposit insurance limits protects savers but also increases the moral hazard that insured banks take greater risks, a cost ultimately borne by the insurance funds and taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The one broadly popular element — raising deposit insurance to $250,000 — was a real protection for ordinary savers, but Congress enacted essentially the same increase in the emergency economic stabilization law that same week, so this bill added nothing on that front. Everything else in the bill — zero capital gains taxes, a lower corporate rate, a discretionary Treasury loan fund for banks, and special loss deductions for Fannie and Freddie preferred stock — directed its benefits toward investors, corporations, and financial institutions, with the cost falling on the Treasury and future taxpayers. Weighed honestly, the bill was dominated by concentrated benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on October 3, 2008, referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees, got no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Aderholt introduced the bill on October 3, 2008, the same day the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act — the $700 billion financial bailout — was signed into law [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee, where jurisdiction was to be split; neither committee took it up [S5].
No member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without any vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers are better off that the bill died: the zero capital gains rate, the corporate rate cut, and the discretionary Treasury loan fund for banks never became law. The popular deposit insurance increase was enacted separately in the bailout bill that week, so savers lost nothing by this bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, since the tax cuts and bank fund died

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the tax provisions; chair Rep. Charles Rangel (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 3, 2008 and never held a hearing or markup on the bill

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the banking provisions; chair Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 3, 2008 and never took the bill up before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in committee in a Democratic-controlled House, so no vote ever revealed a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have given banks low-interest Treasury loans against distressed assets and let them deduct losses on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock against ordinary income, while the higher deposit insurance limit protected their deposit base. The benefits flowed to the institutions while the lending risk fell on taxpayers [S2] [S3].

A zero capital gains rate for individuals and corporations, made permanent by repealing the 2003 rate sunset, would largely benefit households and firms holding appreciated assets, paid for by the general Treasury [S2] [S3].

Eliminating the brackets above 25% and cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 28% would have reduced tax bills for profitable corporations, with the revenue loss borne by other taxpayers [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred shareholders (banks and thrifts)
industries.note: Treating losses on GSE preferred stock as ordinary losses would have given financial institutions larger, more valuable tax deductions on holdings that lost value in the 2008 conservatorship [S3].
